summary: Wilhelm Geiger was an Indologist, Iranian and Central Asian scholar, and linguist. He earned his PhD at Erlangen under Friedrich von Spiegel, later serving as professor at Erlangen (from 1891) and the University of Munich (1920–1924).

Wilhelm Grube worked in Sinology, linguistics, and Tibetology. He studied at Saint Petersburg under Vasilyev and Schiefner, and completed a PhD at Leipzig under Georg von der Gabelentz, later serving as professor of Sinology at the University of Berlin (from 1892).
Wilhelm Gundert was a scholar of Japanology and religious studies who held a post at the University of Hamburg from around 1936 to 1945, where he succeeded Karl Florenz.

Wilhelm Halbfass, an Indologist and philosopher, studied at Vienna and completed his doctorate at Göttingen (~1965–1967). He served as an assistant at Göttingen (~1968–1970) and was a professor at the University of Pennsylvania from 1982 to 2000.

Wilhelm Havers was a linguist and Indologist. His career included posts at the universities of Leipzig (~1913–1915), Bern (~1915–1920), Würzburg (~1920–1929), Breslau (~1929–1937), and Vienna (~1937–1953).

Wilhelm Max Müller was a linguist, historian, and archaeologist. After studying at the universities of Berlin (~1883–1885) and Leipzig (~1885–1888), he held a post at the University of Pennsylvania (~1910–1919).

Wilhelm Pertsch worked in Indology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. He studied at Berlin and Tübingen under Albrecht Weber and Rudolf von Roth, later serving as librarian (from 1855) and director of research institutions at Schloss Friedenstein (from 1883).
Wilhelm Printz was an Indologist who studied under Wilhelm Schulze (~1906–1911) and Heinrich Lüders (~1909–1911).

Wilhelm Radloff specialized in Iranian and Central Asian studies, linguistics, and archaeology. Educated at Berlin and Jena, he directed the Asiatic Museum (1885–1890) and the Kunstkamera (1894–1918), and founded the Russian Museum of Ethnography.

Wilhelm Rau was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at Leipzig under Friedrich Weller and completed his PhD at Marburg under Johannes Nobel, later serving as professor at Frankfurt (1955) and ordinary professor at Marburg (1958–1987).

Wilhelm Scherer was a linguist and literary scholar who studied at Vienna and Berlin. He held chairs at the University of Vienna (1868–1872), the University of Strasbourg (from 1872), and the University of Berlin (from 1877).

Wilhelm Schmidt, a scholar of linguistics and religious studies, studied at the University of Berlin (~1893–1895). He later held posts at the University of Vienna (~1921–1938) and the University of Fribourg (~1939–1951).
Wilhelm Schott worked in Sinology, Iranian and Central Asian studies, and linguistics. After studying at the University of Berlin (~1823–1826), he held a post there from around 1838 to 1889.

Wilhelm Schulze, a linguist and Indologist, studied at Berlin and Greifswald. He held positions at Marburg (1892), a chair in Indo-European linguistics at Göttingen (1895), and a chair at the University of Berlin (1902–1932).
Wilhelm Schüler was a Sinologist who served as a professor at the Seminar for Oriental Languages in Berlin from around 1904 to 1934.

Wilhelm Solf was an Indologist who completed doctoral studies under Richard Pischel (~1883–1885) at Halle-Wittenberg, and also studied at Berlin, Göttingen, Jena, and Kiel. He later held a post at Kiel University.
Wilhelm Storck studied under Franz Bopp from around 1851 to 1854 and under Moriz Haupt from around 1854 to 1857.

Wilhelm Streitberg was a linguist and Indologist who earned his doctorate at Leipzig under Karl Brugmann and Ernst Windisch. He was professor at Fribourg (~1889–1899), Münster (1899), Munich (1909), and Leipzig (1920–1925).

Wilhelm Wackernagel was a linguist who studied at the University of Berlin (1824–1827) under Karl Lachmann and August Boeckh. He subsequently taught at Pädagogium Basel and held a professorship at the University of Basel from 1833, becoming ordinarius in 1835.

Wilhelm Wundt was a philosopher who studied at Tübingen, Heidelberg, and Berlin. He held posts at the University of Zurich (1857), the University of Leipzig (1858), and the University of Heidelberg (1864).
